QF.id: Cat III AIF Fees and Performance_71

question.text: Aarti, a distributor, is comparing two Cat III AIFs - Fund P (Sharpe 1.8, maximum drawdown -12%) and Fund Q (Sharpe 2.2, maximum drawdown -35%). Per the workbook's guidance on evaluating Cat III AIFs (pp. 222 and 224-225), which statement is MOST consistent with the source?

answer.text: Fund Q is unambiguously superior because its Sharpe ratio is higher
Fund Q has a higher Sharpe ratio while Fund P has a materially lower maximum drawdown, so risk-adjusted return AND drawdown should both be evaluated rather than relying on Sharpe in isolation
Fund Q is the safer choice because higher Sharpe means lower total risk
The two funds are functionally identical because Sharpe ratio incorporates drawdown risk

explanation.text: The Logic: Page 222 of the workbook states that higher Sharpe indicates better risk-adjusted return AND warns that risk measures should not be analysed in isolation. Pages 224-225 explain maximum drawdown as peak-to-trough loss - a distinct dimension of tail risk that Sharpe does not capture. Page 340 emphasises matching Cat III AIFs to investor risk appetite. Option B is the source-consistent synthesis: both metrics must be evaluated together rather than declaring one fund "better" purely on Sharpe. The Trap: Option A treats Sharpe as a sole sufficient criterion - directly contradicted by the workbook's warning at p. 222. Option C confuses risk-adjusted return with absolute risk; a higher Sharpe does NOT imply lower drawdown or lower total risk. Option D is factually wrong - Sharpe uses standard deviation, not drawdown. Note: The original item asked which fund was "better" and keyed Fund P, but the workbook does not establish a fund-selection rule based on these two metrics, and Fund Q's higher Sharpe also has partial source backing (p. 222). The stem now asks which statement is source-consistent, allowing a unique non-subjective answer. Source: Series-XIX-B AIF (Category III) Distributors-December workbook, pp. 222, 224-225, 340.
